lesson_headings.1: LESSON — Module 1: Your body in space
lesson_headings.2: LESSON — Module 2: Life aboard the orbital station

mission_heading_template: MISSION — Module {N}. Use your training to handle each situation. There is no time limit.

tasks.title: Pre-flight briefing
tasks.situation: Your spacesuit will be fitted on Earth, but you'll wear it for the first time after three months in orbit. What should the suit technicians plan for?

options.text: Extra length in the torso — you'll probably be a few centimeters taller by then.
The same size — an adult's height doesn't change.
A larger size overall — muscles grow faster in weightlessness.

tasks.title: Day 12 in orbit
tasks.situation: You're choosing food for your personal supply on the next cargo ship. Based on your training, what's the smartest choice?

options.text: Strongly seasoned foods — flavors will seem weaker up here.
Your usual favorite foods — they'll taste the same as at home.
Mostly sweets — sugar is the one taste that gets stronger in orbit.

tasks.title: Day 3 in orbit
tasks.situation: During a video call, your family says: "You look different!" What change are they most likely noticing?

options.text: A rounder, puffier face — and thinner legs, if they could see them.
Nothing much — the body looks the same in orbit; you're just floating.
Much darker skin from the strong sunlight through the station's windows.

tasks.title: Month 6 in orbit
tasks.situation: The flight doctor reviews your latest bone scans. What result should you expect?

options.text: A noticeable loss of bone mass in the hips and spine.
No real change — six months is too short for bones to change.
Denser bones than before launch — floating protects them from wear.

tasks.title: Day 20 aboard the station
tasks.situation: In the science lab, you light a small candle inside a sealed experiment box. What will you most likely see?

options.text: A round, bluish flame.
A normal tall, yellow flame, just like on Earth.
A green flame, because of the station's air filters.

tasks.title: Day 34 aboard the station
tasks.situation: A crewmate gets emotional watching a video message from home. What happens to their tears?

options.text: They collect into a ball of water on the eye.
They roll down the cheeks, the same as on Earth.
They freeze instantly into tiny ice crystals.

tasks.title: Day 41 aboard the station
tasks.situation: You want to photograph every sunrise you can see from the station during one 24-hour period. About how many photos will you take?

options.text: About 16
1 — one sunrise a day, like on Earth
About 100

tasks.title: Day 55 aboard the station
tasks.situation: Mission control asks you to explain the station's water supply to a group of students. What's the most accurate description?

options.text: Almost all of it — about 98% — is recovered and reused, including water from urine and sweat.
Most of it arrives fresh from Earth on cargo ships; only a small part is recycled.
It is made by melting ice collected outside the station.

tasks.title: Sol 47
tasks.situation: You want to photograph tonight's sunset for mission control. What colors should you expect?

options.text: Blue tones.
Deep red and orange, like a sunset on Earth.
Bright green across the whole sky.

tasks.title: Sol 214
tasks.situation: A regional dust storm with winds of about 100 km/h is heading toward your base. What should your crew prioritize?

options.text: Plan to protect and clean the solar panels from dust.
Anchor the habitat and rover — winds this strong could tip them over.
Evacuate to the rover — the storm will make the habitat lose air pressure.

tasks.title: Sol 120
tasks.situation: An outside microphone on your rover records a drill running a few meters away. Compared with the same drill on Earth, what will the recording sound like?

options.text: Quieter — sound travels on Mars, but more weakly and more slowly.
Completely silent — there's no air on Mars for sound to travel through.
Louder — Mars's air carries sound better than Earth's.

tasks.title: Sol 305
tasks.situation: A crewmate is injured, and you need advice from a doctor at mission control. What should you plan for?

options.text: A wait of several minutes — possibly more than 20 — for your message to reach Earth, and as long again for the reply.
A live conversation — radio signals reach Earth within seconds.
No contact at all until the next cargo ship arrives.
